title: Community Update from Mayor Rhodes-Conway (July 31) - City of Madison, WI
text: For Immediate Release July 31, 2026 "There is palpable grief in our community and we must move forward with compassion and grace. I believe Madison can and must do better. A lot better . We need to start that work now. We cannot do that while facing the immediate crisis of an occupation of public spaces. The current blockade of a major thoroughfare detours public bus routes, makes it more difficult for community members to reach their jobs, and impedes fire and EMS response. It is causing real, possibly irreparable, harm to local business owners and community services that remain shut down due to the ongoing occupation.   The people engaging in this activity are members of our community who care about improving Madison and righting legitimate wrongs. But we mustn't squander this energy by abandoning the rule of the law, jeopardizing the livelihoods of our neighbors, and pretending that any single entity, be it City government or someone else, alone, can solve systemic problems overnight. What's currently happening cannot be sustained — in fact, we are wasting precious resources that we need to solve real problems.   The occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street must end. Outreach workers are actively connecting unhoused individuals with services and shelter. There are many opportunities to provide mutual aid to people experiencing homelessness, and I encourage everyone to work with organizations already providing that support. This work can often take time and can be complicated, but we are doing our absolute best to find solutions. What remains true is that this intersection is not a safe location for people to be sleeping in tents, nor for children to play alongside nail-studded blockades.  The life of Corey Ruiz will never be forgotten. The intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street will never be the same. I'm committed to realizing a positive vision in collaboration with Corey's family for a memorial in that space so that our community will never forget. Madison needs more hard conversations, and more hard work, to realize a better future. We must take the first step towards having those conversations in a realistic, non-destructive way. And that starts with voluntarily taking down the barricades, coming together to decide what comes next, and channeling our collective momentum towards a better Madison. I stand ready to work on the next phase. It's time for the barricades to come down." — Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway  Subscribe to the City of Madison News Releases email list. title: EXCLUSIVE: Encampment could cost city ‘hundreds of thousands of dollars,’ mayor says - Channel 3000
text: A full interview with Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway will air Sunday on For the Record. MADISON, Wis. — The encampment at the site where a Madison police officer shot and killed a man could cost the city “hundreds of thousands of dollars,” Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway told News 3 Now on Friday. The encampment at the intersection of Williamson and Baldwin streets was erected late last week in response to the killing of Corey Ruiz. Police said Ruiz was seen “checking vehicles” before his encounter with police and used a knife to injure one of the officers detaining him before the shooting. The City of Madison has provided some resources to keep the protest area safe, including salt trucks parked in front of makeshift barricades. Speaking to News 3 Now, Rhodes-Conway said the trucks were put in place to prevent vehicles from crashing through the barricades and injuring people. “Normally when we would have a protest, or something like this, we would have [police] squad cars down to make sure people were staying safe,” Rhodes-Conway said. “Given the sensitivity of this moment, we’ve chosen to use other city staff and vehicles to do that.” EXCLUSIVE: "I would expect just roughly that we are talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars..." Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway addresses the financial impact of the encampment in her first TV interview since an MPD officer shot and killed a man last week. @WISCTV_News3 pic.twitter.com/WaHbeK9uX4 But utilizing city resources that way can only go on for so long. And for some in the area, the encampment is taking a toll on their patience. Rhodes-Conway issued a statement Thursday calling the encampment neither sustainable nor safe. She said residents in the Marquette neighborhood had reached out to her office with concerns about being unable to sleep, conduct business or safely be in the area. The city is also racking up a massive bill, mostly on overtime and staffing costs, that could have impacts further down the line. “I would expect just roughly that we are talking about hundreds of thousands of dollars,” Rhodes-Conway said. She could not provide an exact number on Friday, but said the total would depend on how long the encampment remains up. She said that the city could be forced to amend its budget due to the spending, but could not yet say what other areas would miss out on funding because of the changes. Madison’s budget is already in a tight spot. The city is already projecting an $11 million gap in its 2027 operating budget, and last month Rhodes-Conway directed all city agencies to cut their budgets by 2%. ​COPYRIGHT 2026 BY CHANNEL 3000. title: Businesses, organizations support Madison community after Corey Ruiz shooting - Spectrum News
text: MADISON, Wis. —  As Madison waits for more information in the investigation into the death of Corey Ruiz, protesters continue to gather at the corner of Williamson and Baldwin streets. In the meantime, local businesses and organizations say they are trying to support the community as people process grief, anger and uncertainty. Videos and images of Ruiz’s death spread widely online in the days after the shooting, adding to the emotional toll for many in the community. Precious Adebayo of the Boys & Girls Clubs of Dane County said the young people she works with have been deeply affected. “They have definitely voiced a lot of feeling unsafe by the people that they feel that they are supposed to reach out for, in order for them to feel safe,” Adebayo said. Adebayo said she and other leaders took a group of teens to the memorial at Williamson and Baldwin, as well as to protests, after they expressed interest in participating. She said it was important to give them a space to process what they were feeling and to advocate for their community. “They want to be heard. They want to be more of an advocate,” she said. Adebayo said the Boys & Girls Club is continuing to serve as a safe space for youth as more information about the shooting becomes public. She also encouraged parents and guardians to give teens room to express themselves. “We want to be able to allow them to share what their feedback is of the situation, let them know that their voices matter and that we are not just listening, but they are heard as well,” Adebayo said. Businesses in the area are also adjusting in response to the aftermath of the shooting. The Madison Public Market had planned to hold its grand opening the day after the shooting, but leaders decided to stay closed after consulting with vendors. “With their guidance, we decided to close in honor and respect for what was happening in the community,” said Keisha Harrison, CEO of the Madison Public Market Foundation. The market later held a quieter opening on Wednesday, with a larger celebration planned for a later date. Harrison said she hopes the space can serve as a place for people to gather, reflect and support local businesses during a difficult time. “What we’re hoping is that people will gravitate towards us to come and have some respite, to have a good time, to have that time for reflection,” Harrison said. In a statement Friday, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said "There is palpable grief in our community and we must move forward with compassion and grace. I believe Madison can and must do better. A lot better. We need to start that work now. We cannot do that while facing the immediate crisis of an occupation of public spaces. The current blockade of a major thoroughfare detours public bus routes, makes it more difficult for community members to reach their jobs, and impedes fire and EMS response. It is causing real, possibly irreparable, harm to local business owners and community services that remain shut down due to the ongoing occupation.” “The occupation at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street must end. Outreach workers are actively connecting unhoused individuals with services and shelter. There are many opportunities to provide mutual aid to people experiencing homelessness, and I encourage everyone to work with organizations already providing that support.” Read the full statement here.

title: Madison police shooting ; mayor says protest site  not sustainable or safe
text: Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issued a statement on Thursday addressing concerns regarding an encampment established to protest the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. MADISON, Wis. - Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway issued a statement on Thursday addressing concerns regarding an encampment established to protest the fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. The mayor called the situation at Williamson and Baldwin streets "not sustainable or safe." "What's happening at the intersection of Williamson Street and Baldwin Street is not sustainable or safe. There are a number of immediate public safety and public health concerns that must not be ignored.  There are not enough bathrooms to support the number of people gathering in that area. There is all-day food preparation taking place without refrigeration, sinks, and other basics. Any time a street is blocked, it can impede fire and EMS response to our community. The middle of city streets is not a safe location for people to be sleeping in tents. Yesterday, a person confronted protesters, started cursing at a large crowd, and pushed people. We have received multiple complaints about people being threatened, from both protesters and neighbors.  We are also hearing from Marquette neighborhood residents that they can't sleep, can't conduct business, are experiencing financial hardships, and can't safely move around the neighborhood. Those who also want real change after the police shooting of Corey Ruiz are increasingly failing to understand and losing patience with a protest tactic that seems misaligned with bringing the community together.  Our first priority needs to be the health and safety of our entire community, and I am asking our entire community to take this seriously and be a part of the solution.   City staff, local elected officials, and neighborhood leaders are continuing to connect with residents and local businesses to address ongoing concerns in the Marquette neighborhood. This work is ongoing and takes many forms. The goal remains to engage residents, community organizers, and the business community to work on a path that prioritizes safety, action, and remembering Corey Ruiz. The City of Madison has published a  FAQ page  to address the common inquiries we have been receiving. We will be updating this page regularly.  The City is also aware of misinformation, rumors, and other falsehoods circulating online and in other venues. Please be careful about sharing information that's not from official sources.  Please reach out if you need help – we all need to take care of ourselves in traumatic times.   The 988 Lifeline is available for immediate support. You can also text HOME or HOLA to 741741 to reach a live crisis counselor.  Public Health Madison Dane County has additional resources   (external) , as well."  Related article Madison police shooting: Department lacks bodycams, stirs debate Wisconsin's largest police departments have body cameras except one – Madison. A new debate erupts over why the city doesn’t have them after last week’s fatal police shooting of Corey Ruiz. The backstory: Madison Police Chief John Patterson said officers responded to calls about a man stealing bicycles and checking car doors and confronted him on July 22, but he rode away on a bicycle. FREE DOWNLOAD: Get breaking news alerts in the FOX LOCAL Mobile app for iOS or Android Police later encountered the man again, at Baldwin and Williamson, and the man "fell or was pulled off the bicycle." There was a struggle in the middle of the intersection, and police said the man pulled out a knife and injured an officer. Officers used a taser to try to take the man into custody before the injured officer shot the man, since identified as Ruiz. Ruiz was pronounced dead at a hospital. Madison police said the four involved officers were placed on administrative leave as the Wisconsin Department of Justice Division of Criminal Investigation investigates the shooting as a homicide .  The Madison Police Department does not have body-worn cameras for officers. After prior efforts to fund bodycams were shut down, Madison Mayor Satya Rhodes-Conway said this week that she will include funding for them in her next budget.
